title: Primed to eat: experimental effects of food marketing on salivation and consumption
official: Taste & mood: exploring physiological and emotional responses to advertisements
summary:
Background and study aims:
Food advertising can influence what people choose to eat and how much they eat. Previous research has suggested that seeing advertisements for food can increase the amount of food people subsequently consume. This evidence has contributed to restrictions on advertising foods that are high in fat, salt and sugar (HFSS) in the UK. However, some forms of food advertising, particularly advertisements that promote food brands rather than specific products, are not covered by the same restrictions.
This study aims to investigate whether different types of food advertising influence people's physical and eating responses. In particular, it will examine whether seeing food advertisements affects how much saliva people produce and how much food they subsequently eat.
The study will compare three types of advertising: advertisements showing a range of food products, advertisements promoting food brands with little or no specific food product imagery, and advertisements for non-food products. By comparing these three groups, the researchers hope to better understand whether different forms of food marketing influence eating behaviour.

Who can participate?
Adults aged 18 years and over from the general public and the University of Liverpool who like the snack food used in the study (Walkers Ready Salted crisps)

What does the study involve?
People interested in taking part will first complete a short screening questionnaire to check whether they meet the eligibility criteria. Those who are eligible will be invited to attend a single session at the University of Liverpool, lasting about 45 minutes. Before starting, participants will receive information about the study and will be asked to provide their informed consent.
Participants will first answer some questions about themselves and complete a short questionnaire about their mood. They will then provide a saliva sample by holding pre-weighed cotton rolls underneath their tongue for 60 seconds.
Participants will subsequently watch a series of short advertisements on a computer screen. They will be randomly allocated to one of three groups, meaning that each participant will see either advertisements for food (brand only) OR food (brand of a range) OR non-food.The advertisements will last about 9 minutes in total.
After watching the advertisements, participants will provide a second saliva sample using the same method. This will allow the researchers to compare the amount of saliva produced before and after watching the advertisements.
Participants will then be offered a portion of Walkers Ready Salted crisps as part of a taste-rating task. They will be free to eat as much or as little as they wish. The researchers will measure how much food has been eaten by weighing the crisps before and after the session.
Participants will also complete a short questionnaire about their mood and take part in an advertisement recognition task to assess which advertisements they remember seeing. Finally, they will be asked some questions about what they think the study was investigating.
At the end of the session, the researcher will explain the true purpose of the study and provide participants with an opportunity to ask questions.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There are no expected direct health benefits from taking part in this study. However, participation will help researchers improve their understanding of how different forms of food advertising may influence eating behaviour. This research may contribute to a better understanding of food marketing and inform future discussions about food advertising and public health.
First-year Psychology students at the University of Liverpool who participate through the department's research participation scheme may receive course credit in recognition of their involvement. Other students and members of the public will be able to contribute to psychological research and gain experience of taking part in a scientific study. No financial payment will be provided for participation.
The study is considered low risk. However, there are some potential risks and minor inconveniences associated with taking part. These include the possibility of choking while eating the crisps, as well as potential discomfort associated with saliva collection or eating the test food. Participants with known food allergies or intolerances will not be eligible to take part. The study will be conducted in a laboratory environment, and appropriate precautions will be taken to minimise potential risks. Participants will also be free to stop taking part at any time if they feel uncomfortable.

Where is the study run from?
University of Liverpool (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
November 2026 to June 2027

Who is funding the study?
University of Liverpool (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Mr Jonathan Oliveira, Jonathan.Oliveira@liverpool.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Aged 18 years or over
2. United Kingdom (UK) resident
3. Fluent in English
4. Self-reported liking of test foods
Exclusion criteria:
1. Dietary restrictions other than vegetarian (e.g., Vegan, gluten-free, sugar-free, dairy/lactose-free)
2. Food allergies/ intolerances (e.g., milk, eggs, nut, wheat, fish etc)
3. Current or historic diagnosed eating disorder
4. Currently dieting
5. Auditory or (non-corrected) vision impairments
6. Taking any medication which may influence taste, salivation or appetite (excluding the contraceptive pill)
7. Current of past diagnosed psychological or mental health condition
8. Smoking (including the use of e-cigarettes)
